wrong: Assigning the security level once upon admission
That is initial classification at reception. Reclassification is the periodic review that follows it.
Transferring an inmate to another facility
A transfer may follow a review, but moving an inmate is not the same as reassessing their classification.
Grouping inmates by the crime committed
Classification weighs risk and needs, not only the offense; reclassification means reviewing that level again over time.
Centralized control of all housing units
Unit management does the opposite: it hands decisions to small units, each with its own staff team.
Rotating guards among housing units daily
Unit management assigns a stable, dedicated team to each unit; daily rotation is what it replaces.
Housing all inmates in one large dormitory
Unit management divides the population into small, semi-autonomous units instead of one large dormitory.
Isolating inmates as a disciplinary penalty
That is disciplinary segregation, a punishment. Protective custody separates inmates to protect them, not to punish them.
Separating sick inmates to prevent contagion
That is medical isolation. Protective custody is for inmates at risk of harm from other inmates.
Holding detainees who await their trial
That describes pre-trial detention, not protective custody.
Static risk factors such as criminal history
Static factors like past offenses cannot change. Criminogenic needs are the dynamic, changeable factors linked to offending.
Basic needs like food, shelter and clothing
Basic needs matter for welfare but are not the crime-related factors that treatment targets.
Health needs met by the prison clinic
Medical needs are non-criminogenic: they do not directly drive criminal behavior.
Silent congregate work by day
That is the Auburn (congregate) system. The Pennsylvania system kept inmates alone day and night.
Progressive stages toward release
That describes the Irish (Crofton) system, not the Pennsylvania separate system.
Earning marks for early release
That is Maconochie's mark system, developed on Norfolk Island.
Solitary confinement day and night with labor
That is the Pennsylvania (separate) system. Auburn let inmates work together in silence.
Open camps with work outside the walls
Open institutions came much later. Auburn was a walled congregate prison.
Progressive stages ending in conditional release
That describes the stages of the Irish system, not the Auburn silent system.
Silent congregate labor in a walled prison
That is the Auburn system. The Irish system moved inmates through stages toward a ticket of leave.
Total solitary confinement for the whole sentence
That is the Pennsylvania system.
Fixed sentences served without any remission
The Irish system rewarded progress with earlier release; fixed terms without remission are the opposite.
Solitary penitence for adult felons
That is the Pennsylvania penitentiary idea. The reformatory movement (Elmira, 1876) targeted young first offenders.
Fixed sentences to deter young offenders
Reformatories used indeterminate sentences tied to reform, not fixed deterrent terms.
Hard labor to repay victims of crime
Restitution through labor is not what defined the reformatory movement.
Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act
That is RA 9344 (2006), later amended by RA 10630.
Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act
That is RA 9165 (2002).
Good Conduct Time Allowance Law
The good conduct time allowance rules were amended by RA 10592 (2013), not RA 10575.
Congregate silent labor and separate cells
That is the Auburn system.
Strict separate confinement for every inmate
That is the Pennsylvania system.
Indeterminate sentences for young first offenders
That is the Elmira reformatory model. The Irish system is the staged progression to a ticket of leave.
Branding offenders to show their past crimes
Branding was an old corporal penalty. The mark system means earning marks (credits) toward release.
Numbering inmates for identification records
Inmate numbers are for identification. The mark system rewards work and conduct with credits.
Fixed release date set by the court at sentencing
The mark system made release depend on the marks earned, not on a fixed date.
First prison to use the Auburn silent system
The silent system began at Auburn Prison, New York (1816). Walnut Street (1790) used solitary cells.
First reformatory for young first offenders
That is Elmira Reformatory (1876).
First federal prison of the United States
Walnut Street was a Philadelphia jail, not a federal prison.
Punishing crime in proportion to its harm
That is the justice (just deserts) model.
Keeping offenders confined to protect society
That is incapacitation, the aim of the custodial model.
Providing hospital care to sick inmates
Prison health care is a service. The medical model treats criminality itself as a condition to diagnose and cure.
Indeterminate Sentence Law
That is Act No. 4103 (1933), which also governs parole.
DILG Act of 1990
That is RA 6975, which created the DILG, PNP, BJMP and BFP.
Juvenile Justice Act of 2006
That is RA 9344.
Probation after prison, parole instead of
Reversed: parole is release after serving part of a prison term; probation is given instead of imprisonment.
Parole is granted by the court, probation by the board
Reversed: probation is granted by the trial court; parole by the Board of Pardons and Parole.
Both are given only after the full sentence
Neither waits for the full sentence: probation replaces prison, and parole is release before the maximum term ends.
Monthly reporting by mail to the officer
That is minimal supervision. Intensive supervision means frequent, close contact.
Release without conditions after sentencing
Probation always has conditions; intensive supervision adds stricter ones.
Confinement in a halfway house at night
That is residential community corrections, not intensive supervision probation.
Recording inmates' calls inside the prison
Call recording is a prison security practice, not electronic monitoring of offenders in the community.
Checking in with an officer by phone weekly
Telephone reporting relies on the offender calling in. Electronic monitoring tracks location with a device.
Watching cell blocks through CCTV cameras
CCTV is institutional surveillance. Electronic monitoring tracks a person, for example with an ankle device, outside prison.
Two sentences served one after the other
That is a consecutive sentence.
Two sentences served at the same time
That is a concurrent sentence.
Sentence divided between two co-accused
Each accused receives their own sentence. A split sentence combines a short jail term with probation for one offender.
Facility where offenders sleep but work outside
That is a halfway house or work-release center; a day reporting center does not involve living there.
Office where probationers report once a month
Monthly reporting is regular probation. A day reporting center requires daily attendance.
Jail where inmates serve weekend sentences
That is intermittent (weekend) confinement.
Crime rises when guardians are absent
That is routine activity theory: a motivated offender, a suitable target and no capable guardian.
Offenders weigh costs and benefits first
That is rational choice theory.
Labeling first offenders deepens deviance
That is labeling theory.
Amnesty is individual, pardon is general
Reversed: a pardon is given to an individual; amnesty is granted to a class of persons, often political offenders.
Pardon needs Congress, amnesty does not
Reversed: amnesty needs the concurrence of a majority of Congress; pardon does not (1987 Constitution, Art. VII, Sec. 19).
Pardon erases the crime, amnesty does not
Reversed: amnesty treats the offense as if it had not been committed; pardon relieves the penalty but not the fact of the crime.
Law allowing probation instead of prison
That is the Probation Law, PD 968.
Law granting deductions for good conduct
Good conduct time allowance is in the Revised Penal Code (Art. 97), as amended by RA 10592.
Law fixing one definite term for every crime
The opposite: Act No. 4103 sets an indeterminate sentence with a minimum and a maximum.
Sentence with one fixed term of years
That is a straight (determinate) penalty.
Sentence served in the community instead
That describes probation or community service, not an indeterminate sentence.
Sentence with no definite end at all
An indeterminate sentence still has a fixed maximum; it is not open-ended.
Focus on curing the causes of offending
That is the medical (rehabilitation) model.
Focus on keeping dangerous people confined
That is incapacitation.
Focus on repairing harm with the victim
That is restorative justice.
Super-maximum, maximum, medium
The Philippines has no super-maximum level; the three levels are maximum, medium and minimum.
Closed, semi-open, open
These are terms used elsewhere. The Bureau of Corrections uses maximum, medium and minimum security.
Maximum, minimum, open
There are three levels and the middle one, medium security, is missing here; 'open' is not one of them.
Medium security for long sentences
Supermax is above maximum security; a long sentence alone does not place an inmate there.
Maximum security for death row only
Supermax holds the most dangerous or disruptive inmates, not only those sentenced to death.
Largest prison by number of inmates
'Supermax' refers to the security level, not the size of the prison.
Monitoring every cell with cameras and motion sensors
That is technical security, part of static security.
Searching cells and inmates without prior warning
Searches are procedural security. Dynamic security relies on staff knowing and talking with inmates.
Rotating staff often so none get close to inmates
That is the opposite: dynamic security depends on staff building working relationships with inmates.
Medical team that treats injured inmates
Medical staff respond to health needs. The emergency response team is a trained unit for riots, disturbances and escapes.
Board that reviews inmate classification
That is the classification board.
Unit that escorts inmates to court hearings
Court escort is a routine transport detail, not the emergency response team.
Staff rapport with inmates
That is dynamic security.
Rules on visits and movement
Rules and routines are procedural security.
Counselling and work programs
Programs support rehabilitation; they are not static security.
Rewarding good conduct with privileges
Rewards alone are behavior modification, such as a token economy. CBT works on the thinking behind behavior.
Exploring childhood conflicts in therapy
That is psychodynamic therapy.
Prescribing medication for behavior
Medication is pharmacological treatment, not cognitive behavioral therapy.
Security classification by escape risk
RNR uses risk to match treatment intensity; it is not a security classification scheme.
Proportionate punishment framework
That is the justice model.
Victim-offender mediation framework
That is restorative justice.
Return of a released inmate to prison
That is recidivism.
Gradual return of inmates to free society
That is reintegration, the opposite direction.
Overcrowding caused by too many admissions
That is congestion. Prisonization (Clemmer) is inmates taking on the prison subculture.
Rehabilitation works for every offender
That is the opposite of Martinson's 1974 'nothing works' conclusion.
Longer sentences reduce reoffending
Martinson reviewed treatment programs; he did not conclude that longer sentences work.
Probation works better than prison
Not the report's conclusion: it found no program that consistently reduced recidivism.
Process of relapsing into crime
That is recidivism.
Process of learning crime from peers
That is differential association.
Process of being labeled a criminal
That is labeling.
Housing unit for inmates under protection
That is protective custody.
Community where parolees must reside
That is a residence condition or a halfway house. A therapeutic community is a structured treatment community, often for drug dependents.
Group of volunteers who visit prisons
Prison volunteers support inmates but are not a therapeutic community.
Medical detoxification under a physician
Detox treats withdrawal. The TC model uses the community itself to change behavior.
Outpatient counselling once a week
That is outpatient care, not a residential therapeutic community.
Confinement of drug users for punishment
The TC model is a treatment approach, not punitive confinement.
Single counselling session per week
A therapeutic milieu uses the whole daily environment, not one session.
Medication as the main treatment tool
That is pharmacological treatment.
Isolation as the main treatment tool
Isolation removes the person from the community, the opposite of a therapeutic milieu.
Private one-on-one counselling sessions
Encounter groups are group sessions in which peers confront each other's behavior.
Recreational group games and sports
Recreation is part of TC life but is not the encounter group.
Family visits supervised by staff
Visits are not encounter groups.
Documenting the victims' injuries at the hospital
Medical documentation records injuries. Reconstruction analyzes the physical evidence to explain how the collision happened.
Taking statements from drivers and witnesses only
Statements are part of the investigation, but reconstruction is the scientific analysis of the physical evidence.
Clearing the road and restoring traffic flow quickly
That is traffic management after the accident.
Examining paint transfer to identify vehicles
That is paint transfer analysis.
Examining glass fragments to find impact point
That is glass fracture analysis.
Measuring road grade to set speed limits
That is traffic engineering, not skid mark analysis.
